Patch-level Kernel Alignment for Self-Supervised Dense Representation Learning

Juan Yeo ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Ijun Jang*    Taesup Kim Affiliation: Gradudate School of Data Science Affiliation: Seoul National University
Abstract

Dense representations are essential for vision tasks that require spatial precision and fine-grained detail. While most self-supervised representation learning methods focus on global representations that summarize the image as a whole, such approaches often fall short in capturing the localized semantics necessary for dense prediction tasks. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework that builds on pretrained representations through additional self-supervised learning, aiming to transfer existing semantic knowledge into the dense feature space. Our method aligns the distributions of dense features between a teacher and a student model. Specifically, we introduce Patch-level Kernel Alignment (PaKA), a simple yet effective alignment objective that captures statistical dependencies, thereby matching the structural relationships of dense patches across the two models. In addition, we investigate augmentation strategies specifically designed for dense representation learning. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art results across a variety of dense vision benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

1 Introduction

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has rapidly advanced the capabilities of vision foundation models, enabling them to learn generalizable visual concepts without reliance on human supervision. While earlier work [1, 2, 3, 4] primarily focused on image-level tasks such as classification, recent studies have shifted toward enabling these models to handle fine-grained, structured tasks, such as semantic segmentation [5, 6, 7] and object detection [8, 9] that require detailed, spatially-aware understanding. Achieving strong performance in such tasks hinges on the quality of dense representations, where each spatial location in the image is embedded with semantically meaningful information.

To enable such dense understanding, recent research has shifted towards dense self-supervised learning, aiming to equip models with fine-grained spatial awareness. Some approaches [10, 11] have advanced dense representation learning by reconstructing masked image patches, showing that high-quality pixel-level features can emerge even without labels. Meanwhile, another line of research [12, 13, 14, 15] has focused directly on learning dense representations using task-specific objectives. For instance, methods like Leopart [15], Croc [14], and CrIBO [12] apply clustering algorithms to group features and train models using clustering-based pseudo-labels. On the other hand, NeCo [13] proposes patch-level consistency objectives built on top of pretrained encoders, enforcing relational structure among local features.

A common thread in these methods is the use of self-distillation, where a student model learns from a teacher. Rather than directly replicating individual dense (i.e., patch-level) feature values, recent approaches [16, 13] focus on learning the structural relationships among dense features, capturing how patches relate to one another across space. In some cases, this extends to aligning the overall distribution of dense features, treating the set of patch embeddings as a population over which meaningful statistical relationships can be modeled. This shift has shown empirical success, as relational consistency offers a more generalizable signal.

Despite the empirical success of relational alignment strategies, many existing methods rely on complex mechanisms such as clustering and patch ranking, often requiring strong assumptions about the underlying feature distribution or extensive hyperparameter tuning. In contrast, we propose PaKA (Patch-level Kernel Alignment), a simple yet principled approach grounded in kernel alignment. Specifically, we employ Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) [17] to align the distributional structure of dense features between teacher and student models. Unlike methods that explicitly model the feature distribution, CKA captures statistical dependencies between feature sets without imposing restrictive distributional assumptions. This enables effective dense feature alignment through a computationally efficient and architecturally lightweight design, free from auxiliary objectives or memory modules.

Furthermore, we revisit augmentation strategies originally designed for image-level self-supervised learning, which have been widely adopted in dense SSL without thorough re-evaluation. Through empirical analysis, we show that certain augmentations commonly used in global representation learning can in fact hinder the learning of spatially precise dense features. Based on these findings, we propose a new cropping strategy tailored for dense representation learning. Our full framework, combining CKA-based alignment and refined augmentation, achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple dense benchmarks, including semantic segmentation and visual in-context reasoning. The main contributions of our work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose Patch-level Kernel Alignment (PaKA), a simple yet effective distribution matching objective that aligns dense features between teacher and student models using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), without relying on clustering, memory banks, or explicit distribution modeling.

  • •

    We analyze the impact of standard augmentation strategies inherited from image-level SSL and identify their limitations for dense representation learning. Based on this analysis, we introduce a new cropping strategy specifically tailored for dense representation learning.

  • •

    We demonstrate that our full framework, which combines CKA-based alignment and refined augmentations, achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse dense vision benchmarks, including semantic segmentation and visual in-context reasoning.

2 Limitations of Distribution Alignment in Dense SSL

Contemporary dense self-supervised learning methodologies [18, 14, 12, 15, 13] approach the problem from the perspective of distribution alignment in feature space. However, existing approaches often impose explicit or implicit constraints on this distribution matching process.

For instance, DenseCL [18] learns patch-level representations using contrastive learning. This method defines a probability distribution for patches under a binary constraint - whether a patch is similar (positive) or dissimilar (negative) to another - and it only leverages these binary relationships during training. Such a limited definition can restrict the diversity of patch relationships captured in the learned distribution.

Cluster-based approaches [12, 14, 15] attempt to partially overcome such limitations by defining the probability distribution of a patch through comparison against KK prototypes, often generated across multiple images. Nevertheless, this approach remains parametric, as it relies on pre-defined parameters such as the number of clusters KK, which constrains the flexibility of the learned distribution.

Similarly, NeCo [13], whose approach of matching relationships among patches within a batch, inherently avoids certain prior parametric limitations (e.g., a pre-defined number of clusters), nonetheless introduces its own form of restriction on the distribution. It establishes a discrete order of similarity among patches via a sorting mechanism. This enforcement of a discrete ranking, by simplifying the potentially continuous spectrum of similarities, can lead to a loss of information and may hinder the learning of more nuanced, fine-grained signals.

To move beyond these approaches, the methodology proposed in this work adopts a non-parametric approach to distribution matching. It learns relationships between patch-level embeddings without imposing any structural priors.

3 Patch-level Kernel Alignment for Dense SSL

We introduce Patch-level Kernel Alignment (PaKA), a simple and flexible framework for dense SSL, as illustrated in Figure 1. PaKA fine-tunes a pre-trained image-level SSL model to learn spatially and semantically rich patch-level representations using a kernel-based alignment loss.

Student–Teacher Learning with Patch-level Representations.

PaKA employs a student-teacher architecture [19], where the teacher network is updated via an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the student. We use Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones initialized from image-level SSL models such as DINOv2 [10]). Our method focuses on further fine-tuning these pretrained models to improve dense representations, in line with previous dense SSL approaches [13, 15]. We apply a multi-crop augmentation strategy [4], generating two global crops VgV_{g} for both networks and multiple low resolution local crops VlV_{l} exclusively for the student. From the global crop VgV_{g}, divided into H×WH\times W patches, the teacher encoder produces a patch-level dense representation Φt∈ℝH×W×D\Phi^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times D}. Similarly, the student encoder processes a local crop and divides into h×wh\times w patches, to yield its patch-level dense representation Φs∈ℝh×w×D\Phi^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times D}. This setup guides the student to learn consistent patch-level representations from semantically constrained local crops, benefiting from the teacher’s more comprehensive view of global crops.

Spatial Alignment via ROI Align.

Due to the differing scales and positions of the global and local crops, the patch-wise outputs Φt\Phi^{t} and Φs\Phi^{s} may not be spatially aligned. To ensure patch-wise comparability for features from these potentially different scaled views, we align representations from the region of intersection between VgV_{g} and VlV_{l}. Specifically, let bb be the bounding box defining VlV_{l} within VgV_{g}. We apply ROI Align to the teacher’s representation Φt\Phi^{t} to extract features corresponding to this intersection, resized to a target h′×w′h^{\prime}\times w^{\prime} grid: Φbt=ROIAlign​(Φt,b,h′,w′)\Phi^{t}_{b}=\text{ROIAlign}(\Phi^{t},b,h^{\prime},w^{\prime}). Similarly, the student’s representation Φs\Phi^{s} is resized to Φbs=ROIAlign​(Φs,b,h′,w′)\Phi^{s}_{b}=\text{ROIAlign}(\Phi^{s},b,h^{\prime},w^{\prime}). This results in two aligned feature maps, Φbt,Φbs∈ℝh′×w′×D\Phi^{t}_{b},\Phi^{s}_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{h^{\prime}\times w^{\prime}\times D}, which are subsequently flattened into N=h′×w′N=h^{\prime}\times w^{\prime} patch embeddings:

T=[𝐭1,…,𝐭N]⊤,S=[𝐬1,…,𝐬N]⊤∈ℝN×D.T=[\mathbf{t}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{t}_{N}]^{\top},\quad S=[\mathbf{s}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{s}_{N}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}.

The aligned patch embeddings, TT and SS, are dense features that represent the same overlapping region captured from different views. Given the inherently complex and high-dimensional nature of these patch-derived feature sets, TT and SS, it is crucial to adopt an alignment methodology that can effectively capture their intricate relational structures.

Kernel-based Relational Alignment.

PaKA’s core idea is to achieve this alignment of TT and SS using kernel-based methods. In the context of transferring knowledge by alinging feature distributions, kernel-based strategies [20, 21, 22, 23, 24] offer a distinct advantage over pairwise or triplet-based approaches [25, 26]. While the latter provide a limited view on feature relationships, kernel methods facilitate a more holistic comparison by enabling the alignment of entire similarity structures, typically represented by Gram matrices. Specifically for our dense SSL scenario, we construct Gram matrices Kt=T​T⊤K^{t}=TT^{\top} and Ks=S​S⊤K^{s}=SS^{\top} using linear kernels applied to the patch-level feature embeddings TT and SS. These matrices encapsulate the pairwise similarity structure within each feature set.

To robustly align the relational structures captured by these Gram matrices, KtK^{t} and KsK^{s}, we specifically employ Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). This decision is based on compelling advantages critical for our dense SSL task. Firstly, CKA is fundamentally rooted in the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) [27], allowing it to assess the statistical dependence between the feature distributions represented by KtK^{t} and KsK^{s}. This facilitates a meaningful comparison of their underlying similarity structure, even when the teacher and student networks produce features that are distanced from each other. Secondly, CKA’s methodology, which involves centering the kernel matrices and normalizing the HSIC value, renders it invariant to isotropic scaling of the input features. The effectiveness of CKA in capturing and aligning similarity structures has been demonstrated in domains such as knowledge distillation [23, 24] and self-supervised learning [21], underscoring its suitability for effectively aligning the dense feature representations TT and SS within our PaKA framework.

Relational Alignment via Centered Kernel Alignment.

The CKA-based alignment of the global geometry between the patch-level representations TT and SS is implemented as follows. Starting with the Gram matrices KtK^{t} and KsK^{s}, which are derived using linear kernels as previously defined, we first center them using the centering matrix H=I−1N​𝟏𝟏⊤H=I-\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}:

K~s=H​Ks​H,K~t=H​Kt​H.\tilde{K}^{s}=HK^{s}H,\quad\tilde{K}^{t}=HK^{t}H.

The CKA similarity, which quantifies the likeness between the representations S and T using their centered Gram matrices, is then defined as:

CKA​(S,T)=⟨K~s,K~t⟩F‖K~s‖F⋅‖K~t‖F.\text{CKA}(S,T)=\frac{\langle\tilde{K}^{s},\tilde{K}^{t}\rangle_{F}}{\|\tilde{K}^{s}\|_{F}\cdot\|\tilde{K}^{t}\|_{F}}.

The CKA metric quantifies the dependency between kernels: a high CKA means strong dependency, while a low CKA implies weak dependency. Consequently, for a loss function, we desire a formulation where minimizing the loss corresponds to increasing CKA. As CKA is normalized between 0 and 1, the loss term takes the form of 1−C​K​A1-CKA, effectively converting the maximization of CKA into a minimization problem. The PaKA loss is:

ℒPaKA=1−CKA​(S,T).\mathcal{L}_{\text{PaKA}}=1-\text{CKA}(S,T).

Our PaKA loss has a value between 0 and 1 and does not require any hyperparameters. Minimizing this loss encourages the student to preserve the teacher’s pairwise patch relationships, offering robust alignment without forcing 𝐬i≈𝐭i\mathbf{s}_{i}\approx\mathbf{t}_{i} directly.

Cross-image Generalization and Scalability.

To enhance diversity and generalization, PaKA computes Gram matrices over the union of all patch features from multiple images in a mini-batch. This encourages learning relational structures consistent both within and across instances, improving semantic organization and scalability without additional design overhead.

4 Revisiting Augmentation Strategies for Dense SSL

Data augmentation is pivotal in self-supervised learning (SSL), defining invariances for the model. However, dense SSL has largely inherited augmentation strategies from image-level SSL. We critically examine these for dense learning and propose strategies better suited to patch-level representation alignment, as illustrated in 2(a).

From Image-level to Dense-level Augmentation.

Image-level SSL methods [1, 3, 4, 19] use augmentations (e.g., multi-crop) to create different "views" for instance-level invariance. Teacher-student frameworks (e.g., BYOL [3], DINO [19]) often provide the teacher one global view, while the student receives global and multiple smaller local views [4]. Dense SSL methods like NeCo [13] and Leopart [15] retained this paradigm, feeding global crops to both student and teacher, with spatial alignment via ROI Align for local views. This approach has limitations for dense feature alignment:

  • •

    Local crops often have minimal spatial overlap with global crops, reducing mutual information and alignment utility.

  • •

    Strong augmentations on the teacher view may introduce noise, leading the student to overfit to non-semantic artifacts.

To address this, we introduce two key augmentation refinements.

Towards Overlap-aware View Sampling.

Dense SSL methods [15, 13] compute their objective by applying ROI Align exclusively to the overlapping regions of patches derived from global and local crops of differing sizes. A critical issue arises in this process: if the spatial overlap between these global and local crops is minimal, the amount of information incorporated into the loss function diminishes significantly, which can hinder effective learning. To maximize shared information between teacher and student views, we propose Global–Local Intersection Maximization: enforcing a minimum spatial Intersection-over-Union (IoU) between local and global crops. Given fixed crop sizes (e.g., global 518×518518\times 518, local 98×9898\times 98 as in NeCo [13]), we reject local crops whose IoU with the corresponding global crop is below a threshold ratio mm. Controlling this minimum overlap mm explicitly regulates mutual information. Empirically, increasing mm consistently improves clustering performance (2(b), confirming denser shared regions lead to more effective alignment. In our method, we set the value of mm to ensure an overlap of 90% or greater.

Reducing Noise with an Augmentation-free Teacher.

Effective dense SSL hinges on capturing fine-grained spatial relationships, not just global semantics, which fundamentally reframes the teacher’s role from simply another augmented peer to a stable semantic anchor. Contrary to common practice in some prior dense SSL methods where the teacher also undergoes strong augmentation, we introduce a clean-teacher strategy: the teacher receives an unaugmented or very weakly transformed image, while the student still processes the full augmentation pipeline. Our Clean Teacher Strategy embodies this revised role through an asymmetric configuration: the student learns invariance from strong augmentations while aligning to a teacher that ideally processes an entirely augmentation-free input. This ensures the teacher provides exceptionally reliable signals reflecting the image’s intrinsic structure. Our experiments in 2(c) compellingly support this, showing that student representation quality is highest when all augmentations, including color jitter and blur, are removed from the teacher’s pipeline.

5 Experiments

We assessed the quality of representations learned by our approach through tasks that operate directly within the embedding space with minimal supervision, such as visual in-context learning and overclustering. We also investigate the transferability and robustness of these features in scenarios by linear semantic segmentation and end-to-end finetuning with a linear head. Furthermore, we examine the adaptability of our method when integrated with a variety of pretrained backbone models.

5.1 Setup

Datasets.

We use the COCO [29] dataset for model training, with evaluation conducted across a diverse set of datasets, including Pascal VOC 2012 [28], COCO [29], Pascal Context [30], ADE20K [31], COCO-Stuff 164K [32]. These datasets cover various tasks in this study. For visual in-context learning, performance is measured using Pascal VOC 2012 and ADE20K. For the overclustering task, we follow previous work [15], employing Pascal VOC 2012 and Pascal Context. For semantic segmentation, we report both linear-probe and full fine-tuning results on Pascal VOC 2012, Pascal Context, ADE20K, and COCO-Stuff 164K.

Implementation Details.

The training is conducted using 4 RTX 3090 GPUs with 24GB of memory in a mini-batch size of 10 for each GPU. For a fair comparison, NeCo [13] was also trained under identical hardware and batch size configurations based on the code from official GitHub repositories. We use AdamW [33] optimizer with a learning rate of 1​e−61\mathrm{e}{-6} for backbone model, a weight decay of 0.04, and 20 workers. Our models, post-trained from pretrained checkpoints, generally underwent 25 epochs of training, with the exception of a 10 epochs schedule for data augmentation experiments. For DINOv2 [10] we use 518×\times518 for global crops and 98×\times98 for local crops.

5.2 Comparison with Prior Works

Visual In-Context Learning.

We evaluate our method using the visual in-context reasoning benchmark [35] which is inspired by natural language processing (NLP). This benchmark assesses a vision encoder’s scene understanding capabilities directly from its learned representations, without relying on decoders or parameter tuning. Essentially, the benchmark performs patch-level nearest neighbor retrieval. Dense representations extracted from validation set images serve as queries and keys for retrieval are constructed from training images. The training images are uniformly sampled subsets of the training set, with sub-sampling rates of 1, 8, 64 or 128. Patches from these selected training images are then encoded and stored in a memory bank, and label for a given query patch is subsequently predicted by leveraging the labels of its nearest neighbors retrieved from this memory bank.

We applied our method for post-training, starting from pretrained models DINOv2R, and PaKA outperformed most of the methods in Table 1. On average, PaKA improved the performance of DINOv2R by 3.5% in PascalVOC. The high performance of PaKA in visual in-context learning suggests that our method excels at extracting semantically more similar features from the memory bank, which is a collection of features serving as a surrogate for the vast feature space.

Overclustering.

The quality of the dense representations is further assessed using an overclustering task that requires minimal additional supervision similar to visual in-context learning. Following the previous work [15], we apply KK-means clustering via Faiss [36] to all dense features from the backbone, explicitly discarding the projection head. The generated clusters are greedily matched to ground-truth classes at the pixel level, followed by a Hungarian matching [34] to ensure permutation-invariant [37] evaluation. Performance is quantified using mIoU and assessed at various granularities, with KK set to the number of ground-truth objects as well as overclustering values of 300 and 500.

As shown in Table 2, PaKA achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets. In particular, for PascalVOC with K=500K=500, the post-trained NeCo model improves upon the DINOv2R baseline by 21.2 %, whereas PaKA attains a 38.9 % gain. This represents a 17.7 % absolute advantage over NeCo, which is an another post-training method. Such a margin suggests that PaKA learns features that are well-distributed in cluster-level within the feature space.

Linear Semantic Segmentation.

To assess the generalization capabilities of the learned representations, we perform linear semantic segmentation. This involves keeping the backbone weights frozen and attaching a linear classification head. The head projects dense features from backbone to class logits, which are resized to the input resolution through bilinear interpolation to match the target masks. We compute pixel-level cross-entropy loss for supervision and report mIoU performance on four standard segmentation benchmarks. This approach directly evaluates the discriminative power of the static pretrained features, offering insights into their quality without task-specific adaptation of the backbone.

In Table 3, PaKA outperforms by an average of 6.7 % across all four benchmarks more than DINOv2R. Notably, on ADE20K—arguably challenging dataset because of its diverse object categories and complex scene layouts—PaKA achieves the largest absolute gain, surpassing NeCo by 3.1 %. This demonstrates that PaKA still delivers the bigger boost, underscoring its superior ability to learn highly transferable, discriminative features without any task-specific fine-tuning of the backbone.

End-to-End Finetuning with a linear head.

To evaluate the transferability of pretrained features in an end-to-end setup, we finetune the entire network including the backbone and linear head. The model is trained using a pixel-wise cross-entropy loss, and final performance is reported using mIoU on Pascal VOC 2012, Pascal Context, COCO-Stuff 164K, and ADE20K.

After end-to-end fine-tuning, PaKA attains the highest mIoU scores on every benchmark compared to all dense self-supervised methods in Table 4. These consistent gains demonstrate that PaKA is a strong, task-agnostic initialization for dense prediction tasks. Even more surprisingly, the post-training method NeCo actually degrades the performance of its underlying pretrained model, while our approach constantly improves the preformance of DINOv2R.

Adapting to Diverse Pretrained Backbones.

In Table 5, we investigate the adaptability of our method to different pretrained backbones originating from diverse self-supervised learning strategies. We test our approach on a model initialized with iBOT [11], DINO [19], CrIBo [12].

On overclustering and linear segmentation task, PaKA raises average mIoU by 10.9 % when starting from iBOT, by 16.1% when starting from DINO, and by 4.5% when starting from CrIBo. The largest gains occur on DINO, an image-level pretrained model, showing that PaKA can convert image-level pretrained model to do dense-prediction representations. At the same time, other methods which is pretrained in dense self-supervised scheme, still benefits from PaKA’s post-training refinement, confirming that PaKA not only unlocks dense capability for image-level models but also polishes the spatial quality of models that are already densely trained.

5.3 Ablation Study

To validate the design choices of our proposed Patch-level Kernel Alignment (PaKA) framework and to understand the individual contributions of its key components, we conduct a series of ablation studies. All studies are evaluated in the Pascal VOC 2012 and ADE20k datasets, reporting performance in overclustering tasks (K=500K=500) and linear semantic segmentation tasks.

Impact of Kernel Alignment Metric.

We ablated the choice of kernel alignment metric, comparing our Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) against Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC). 6(a) reveals that CKA consistently achieves the highest scores in across all datasets. This superior performance underscores CKA’s greater efficacy in aligning dense feature distributions between teacher and student models, validating its use in PaKA.

Patch Grouping Strategy for Kernel Construction.

We investigated patch combination strategies for kernel construction, comparing our chosen inter-image sampling with intra-image and hybrid approaches. 6(b) shows that intra-image strategy leads to markedly poor performance, lower than the initial pretrained model. Focusing solely on similar patches from the same image, intra-image sampling restricts the model’s understanding of diverse feature structures. In contrast, both inter-image and hybrid sampling significantly outperform this approach, with inter-image achieving the highly competitive results across Pascal VOC and ADE20k. This highlights the importance of incorporating patch diversity from multiple images for robust kernel alignment, validating our choice of inter-image sampling for PaKA.

Efficacy of Proposed Augmentation Strategies.

Our ablation study assesses two strategies, maximizing global-local intersection (Max.) and a clean teacher (Clean.), against a baseline of standard augmentations [15] combined with the CKA loss. While 6(c) shows both provide individual gains, the maximizing intersection strategy’s contribution is comparatively modest. This may be because standard augmentations already provide a mean view overlap of 75.5% (measured across 300 COCO samples), whereas our strategy enforces an even stricter ≥\geq90% overlap to maximize shared information. Importantly, combining two augmentation strategies delivers the highest overall performance, demonstrating their synergistic benefits.

Effectiveness of Our Augmentation Strategy.

We conducted a cross-combination study to evaluate the interplay between alignment losses, specifically our PaKA versus sorting-based loss of NeCo [13], and augmentation strategies, comparing our proposed method against standard augmentation [15]. 6(d) indicates that our proposed augmentation improves NeCo’s sorting loss by +1.3% and +0.9% in overclustering on Pascal VOC and ADE 20k. Notably, even when paired with standard augmentation, PaKA loss with standard augmentation already outperforms this enhanced NeCo performance. best results across all datasets are achieved by combining PaKA loss with our proposed augmentation, highlighting their combined strength.

6 Conclusion

We presented a novel framework that significantly advances dense self-supervised learning by overcoming key limitations of existing methods. Our core contribution, PaKA, introduces kernel alignment for effective teacher-student dense feature structure transfer, utilizing Centered Kernel Alignment for efficient, assumption-free distributional matching. PaKA notably circumvents the need for auxiliary components such as iterative clustering, memory banks, or sorting algorithms, thereby reducing the training complexity and hyperparameter sensitivity frequently associated with these prior mechanisms. This streamlined approach, combined with our augmentations, establishes a robust framework achieving state-of-the-art performance on tasks requiring detailed spatial understanding, paving the way for more accessible and scalable dense SSL.

Appendix A Additional Remarks and Disclosures

A.1 License information of the assets used in this work

We report known license information of the assets used in this work. The following datasets under the MIT License are used in this paper: ADE20K [31]. The following datasets under the CC BY 4.0 License are used in this paper: COCO [29], COCO Stuff [32]. The following datasets used in this paper are for research purpose only (term of access): ImageNet [38], PASCAL VOC 2012 [28].

A.2 Limitations

Our work proposes a principled yet simple approach for dense representation learning through distribution matching. However, we acknowledge that PaKA does not provide a formal theoretical justification for why aligning patch-level similarity structures via CKA leads to improved spatial understanding. This limitation is not unique to our work—most existing dense SSL frameworks [15, 12, 13] rely on empirical validation rather than grounded theory. A deeper theoretical study of how and why distribution alignment affects dense learning remains an open and important direction for the field.

In addition, while PaKA demonstrates that strong performance can be achieved without complex components like clustering algorithms or memory banks, the framework currently operates in a relatively constrained setting. We believe that PaKA could serve as a strong base upon which more sophisticated modules—such as attention-guided augmentation, region-aware alignment, or semantic prototypes—can be layered to achieve even greater accuracy and robustness.

A.3 Broader Impact

Our work introduces PaKA, a lightweight and efficient framework that enhances the fine-grained understanding capabilities of existing vision foundation models through a simple yet principled self-supervised learning objective. Unlike prior dense SSL methods that rely on complex mechanisms such as clustering, patch ranking, or large memory banks, PaKA leverages the Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) metric to align patch-level feature distributions in a hyperparameter-free and architecturally minimal manner. This simplicity enables scalable and resource-efficient adaptation of pretrained vision models to dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation and visual reasoning, without requiring large-scale labeled datasets or significant computational overhead.

The broader societal impact of our method lies in its potential to democratize high-quality dense vision understanding. By enabling fine-grained spatial reasoning with minimal resources, PaKA lowers the barrier for deploying advanced vision models in real-world applications such as medical imaging, autonomous navigation, and remote sensing, where annotated data is scarce and computational budgets are limited. Furthermore, the efficiency and simplicity of our method may accelerate innovation in settings like mobile or embedded vision systems, ultimately supporting more accessible and sustainable AI development.

Appendix B Related Works

B.1 Image-level Self-supervised Learning

Self-supervised learning (SSL) for image representation has progressed from pretext tasks [39, 40, 41, 42], such as solving jigsaw puzzles [40] or predicting rotations [39]. Contrastive learning [1, 2, 43] subsequently achieved substantial gains by explicitly learning to differentiate augmented views of an instance from those of other instances, though often at the cost of requiring numerous negative samples. This challenge motivated non-contrastive methods [44, 3], which employed techniques like exponential moving average (EMA) updates to a target network, effectively avoid trivial solutions without explicit negative pairs. While contrastive and non-contrastive approaches primarily operate on the similarity between individual image instances, clustering-based methods [45, 46, 4] were proposed to capture higher-level semantics in feature groups. Especially, SwAV [4] introduced online clustering mechanisms coupled with multi-crop augmentation. This augmentation strategy became foundational for subsequent works like DINO [19], which interprets SSL via a self-distillation framework where a student network learns from a teacher network.

B.2 Dense Self-Supervised Learning

Dense self-supervised learning methods [47, 48, 10, 49, 18, 11, 16] aim to capture fine-grained, spatially-aware representations, which is an essential aspect for many vision tasks. Initial adaptations, similar to image-level contrastive approaches [1, 2], saw methods like DenseCL [18] adapting contrastive objectives to the local feature level. Subsequently, a major line of work emerged in clustering-based methods [12, 14, 15], where dense features are grouped to form object-level representations without supervision. Leopart [15] notably combined a dense clustering objective with the framework of DINO [19], including its multi-crop and teacher-student strategies to improve pretrained models. The field further evolved by incorporating retrieval mechanisms, often with a memory bank [50]. Hummingbird [51] employed dense nearest-neighbor retrieval for in-context learning, and CriBo [12] extended this to cluster-level cross-image retrieval to enhance semantic consistency. In contrast, NeCo [13] uses patch-level retrieval to refine image-level pretrained models with a sorting-based objective.
However, the reliance of these methods on memory banks, clustering, or sorting algorithms often increases training complexity and can be sensitive to hyperparameter choices. Our work addresses these challenges by introducing a kernel alignment method for effective teacher-student dense feature structure transfer, offering a simple and effective framework that circumvents the need for auxiliary components.

B.3 Kernel Alignment

The challenge of transferring complex representational structures between models has been widely explored in knowledge distillation (KD) [52, 20, 53, 25, 26, 23]. Some works [25, 26] align pairwise feature relationships by comparing distances and angles between features. These pairwise or triplet-based approaches have limited capacity to capture the full structure of a teacher’s feature manifold. Kernel-alignment methods [20, 21, 22, 23, 24] emerged as a more powerful solution, enabling the comparison and alignment of entire similarity structures via gram matrix alignment in high-dimensional spaces. FKD [20] advances this idea further by treating the neural network itself as a data-dependent kernel and defining feature kernels directly from its activations. As kernel is sensitive to feature scale, [24] applies Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) [17] on mini-batches which is invariant to scaling and [23] further analyze why CKA is effective in knowledge distillation. SSL-HSIC [21] interprets Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) [27] as InfoNCE and propose maximizing kernel dependence maximization between image features and one-hot encoded labels for SSL.
While existing works primarily target global or instance-level features, our method is specifically designed to align intricate, spatially correlated dense feature maps. We propose a tailored approach to define and align kernel matrices from these dense structures, enabling an efficient transfer of fine-grained spatial relationships from teacher to student encoders.

Appendix C Experimental Results

Towards Overlap-aware View Sampling.

To quantify how much spatial correspondence matters, we vary the minimum Intersection-over-Union (IoU) between global and local crops while keeping their absolute sizes fixed. As shown in Table 7, raising the overlap threshold from the 0.10.1–0.30.3 band to 0.90.9–1.01.0 yields a consistent mIoU gain. These results validate our Global–Local Intersection Maximization: enforcing m≥0.9m\geq 0.9 ensures that teacher and student views share sufficiently dense context, thereby injecting more mutual information into the loss and driving better alignment.

Reducing Noise with an Augmentation-free Teacher.

Next, we decouple augmentation strengths for the teacher and student branches. Table 8 reveals a clear trend: the less noise the teacher sees, the higher the downstream clustering quality. Completely disabling teacher augmentations while leaving the student fully augmented (0/10/1) produces the best score at every K (e.g., 73.68 at K=500K=500). Even partial clean-teacher settings (0/0.60/0.6 or 0/00/0).

Appendix D Experimental Setup

D.1 Dense Self-Supervised Learning

Dataset.

The pretraining datasets employed in this study include COCO. The COCO dataset, specifically, comprises approximately 118,000 scene-centric images.

Network Architecture.

For the architectural backbone, ViTs are utilized. More specifically, models are trained using the ViT-Small and ViT-Base architectures. Furthermore, adopting the methodologies [19, 3], a student-teacher learning paradigm is implemented. Within this framework, the teacher model parameters are updated via an EMA of the student model’s parameters.

Removing registers in Dinov2.

Our Primary experiments are based on DINOv2XR, removing the registers from the DINOv2R [54] to restore the original DINOv2 [19] patch-based input structure. Unless noted otherwise, all ablation studies and hyperparameter searches are likewise carried out on the DINOv2XR backbone.

Optimization.

The models were trained on four NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs (each with 24GB of VRAM), utilizing a mini-batch size of 10 per GPU. Optimization was performed using the AdamW [33] optimizer. The learning rate for the backbone model was set to 1​e−61\mathrm{e}{-6}, with a weight decay of 0.040.04. Data loading was facilitated by 20 worker processes. The exponential moving average that updates the teacher’s weights follows a cosine schedule, increasing from an initial value of 0.990.99 to a value of 11. Our models, initialized from pretrained checkpoints, were generally post-trained for 25 CoCo epochs. However, for experiments specifically focused on data augmentation, we trained 10 epochs. Based on  [19], we employ a three-layer projection head with 2,048 hidden units per layer, Gaussian error linear unit activations [55], and an output dimension of 256.

Data Augmentation.

Dense SSL methods [15, 13] create different views using augmentations (e.g., multi-crop), provide the teacher one global view, while the student receives global and multiple local views. When employing the DINOv2 [10] framework, input images were processed into global crops of 518×518518\times 518 pixels and local crops of 98×9898\times 98 pixels. To enhance dense feature alignment for our COCO pretraining, we introduce crucial refinements to this process. Specifically, we set the teacher’s augmentation strength to 0 to provide a noise-free target, while applying standard augmentations to the student’s views with a strength of 1. Furthermore, to maximize mutual information and ensure local views are strongly anchored within the global context, we enforce a strict overlap requirement, ensuring that the intersection area between a teacher’s global crop and any corresponding local crop must exceed 0.90.9.

D.2 Evaluation Setup

Visual In-Context Learning.

Our evaluation methodology adheres to the visual in-context reasoning benchmark proposed by [51], designed to assess the scene understanding capabilities of vision encoders directly from their learned representations without necessitating decoders or subsequent parameter adjustments. The core of this benchmark involves a patch-level nearest neighbor retrieval process. Dense representations extracted from validation set images serve as queries. The keys for retrieval are constructed from training images, which are uniformly sub-sampled from the complete training set at fractions of 11 (full set), 1/81/8, 1/641/64, or 1/1281/128. Patches derived from these chosen training images are then encoded and compiled into a memory bank. The label for any given query patch is subsequently inferred by leveraging the labels of its nearest neighbors retrieved from this memory bank. We utilized the open implementation by [56], which is faithful to the original description by [51] and employs the ScaNN library [57] for efficient neighbor searches. Consistent with the setup for the [51], we used a memory size of 10,240,000 and configured ScaNN to retrieve 30 nearest neighbors. Final performance is reported as mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on subsets of Pascal VOC 2012 [28] and ADE20K [31] datasets.

Overclustering.

To evaluate unsupervised segmentation quality via overclustering, we adopted the protocol from Leopart [15]. The procedure commences with feature extraction: spatial tokens are gathered from the model’s backbone using input images standardized to 448×448448\times 448 crops. These tokens then undergo KK-Means clustering, for which the faiss [36] implementation is employed. The crucial step of achieving permutation invariance, as emphasized by [37], is realized by applying the Hungarian algorithm [34]. This algorithm operates on cluster maps that are initially formed through a greedy matching process based on pixel-level precision. To ensure the computational feasibility of the Hungarian matching, the overclustering is performed on 100×100100\times 100 downsampled masks. Final assessment metrics are reported as the average mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) from five runs with different random seeds, on the COCO-Thing [32], Pascal VOC 2012 [28], and ADE20K [31] datasets.

Linear Semantic Segmentation.

The linear semantic segmentation evaluation followed the setup established in Leopart [15]. The process of generating predictions began with 448x448 input images, which were fed into our backbone model to obtain spatial output features. These features were then resized using bilinear interpolation to align with the dimensions of the target segmentation masks. A linear classification head was subsequently applied to these processed features to yield the final segmentation predictions. The training of this linear head was driven by a cross-entropy loss, calculated between the predictions and the ground-truth masks. The optimization was performed using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with specific hyperparameters: a weight decay of 0.00010.0001, momentum of 0.90.9, and a learning rate of 0.010.01. The linear head was fine-tuned over 20 epochs. We trained and evaluated these linear heads on Pascal VOC 2012 [28], COCO-Thing and COCO-Stuff [32], and ADE20K [31] datasets.

End-to-End Finetuning with a linear head.

The end-to-end finetuning segmentation approach builds upon the previously detailed linear evaluation setup, retaining most of its core configurations. However, in this mode, we fine-tuned the entire model, thereby jointly optimizing the parameters of the feature-extracting backbone and the linear head. To facilitate this full network training, the backbone was finetuned using a learning rate of 0.00010.0001, and the linear head was simultaneously trained with a learning rate of 0.010.01. The fine-tuning process was conducted for 20 epochs, with performance evaluated as mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on Pascal VOC 2012 [28], COCO-Thing and COCO-Stuff [32], and ADE20K [31] datasets.

Appendix E Additional Experiments

E.1 VIT-B Model Performance

To demonstrate the robustness and broader applicability of our proposed Patch-level Kernel Alignment (PaKA) framework, this section presents an evaluation of its performance when applied to the ViT-B architecture. The ViT-B model was trained with settings identical to ViT-S, with the exception of the batch size, which was set to 5 for ViT-B due to the memory constraints.

Visual In-Context Learning on ViT-B.

The visual in-context learning results presented in Table 9 highlight the significant benefits of leveraging the larger ViT-B architecture with our PaKA framework, which not only yields overall performance gains over PaKA with ViT-S, but also markedly outperforms other methods. When compared to other methods employing the ViT-B backbone, PaKA consistently achieves the highest performance across all data regimes on both ADE20K and Pascal VOC datasets. This includes outperforming the prior post-training method NeCo (ViT-B), for example, by 4.5% (1/1281/128) and 3.8% (1/641/64) on Pascal VOC. Such strong performance highlights that PaKA effectively learns a feature space well-structured for nearest-neighbor based scene understanding.

Overclustering on ViT-B.

In overclustering, leveraging the larger ViT-B/14 architecture with our PaKA framework leads to notable performance gains over PaKA with ViT-S/14. Crucially, PaKA trained on this ViT-B model achieves the highest mIoU scores across all benchmarks compared to other methods. Table 10 details the overclustering performance, where leveraging the ViT-B/14 architecture with our PaKA framework brings. Notably, on COCO-Things dataset with K=500, PaKA achieves a remarkable mIoU gain, surpassing the DINOv2R baseline by over 33.6. This large performance gain, especially on COCO-Things, underscores PaKA’s effectiveness in learning features that naturally align with semantic boundaries, proving its ability to produce high-quality, clusterable dense representations.

Linear Semantic Segmentation on ViT-B.

In linear semantic segmentation, leveraging the larger ViT-B/14 architecture with our PaKA framework leads to notable performance gains over PaKA with ViT-S/14. Crucially, PaKA trained on this ViT-B model achieves the highest mIoU scores across all benchmarks compared to other methods in  Table 11. Using the ViT-B backbone, PaKA demonstrates a consistent advantage, achieving an average mIoU gain of 3.4 over DINOv2R across the benchmarks.

End-to-End Finetuning Segmentation on ViT-B.

When the entire network is finetuned for semantic segmentation, PaKA’s ViT-B initialization proves superior. Crucially, PaKA trained on this ViT-B model achieves the highest mIoU scores across all benchmarks compared to other methods. Following  Table 12, this advantage is particularly pronounced on the challenging COCO-Stuff and ADE20K datasets. On COCO-Stuff, PaKA reaches 64.8%, and on ADE20K, it achieves 48.4%, setting new state-of-the-art results in both cases and clearly outperforming NeCo. This demonstrated that PaKA generalize and learn robust features applicable to diverse and complex semantic segmentation tasks.

E.2 Diverse Pretrained Backbones

We applied PaKA into different backbones initialized with different pretraining methods. The linear segmentation results, presented in Table 13, show that PaKA consistently and significantly improves performance across all four benchmark datasets. Notably, when PaKA is applied to an image-level pretrained model, DINO [19], it yields substantial gains, such as +15.0+15.0 mIoU on Pascal VOC and +17.4+17.4 mIoU on COCO-Things. Furthermore, PaKA also enhances models already pretrained with dense SSL objectives. For instance, it improves iBOT [11] by +4.0+4.0 mIoU on Pascal VOC and +7.9+7.9 mIoU on ADE20K, and improves CrIBo [12] by +5.1+5.1 mIoU on COCO-Stuff and +6.2+6.2 mIoU on ADE20K. This consistent uplift underscores PaKA’s ability to effectively refine and adapt features for dense prediction tasks.

E.3 Computational Cost

Our proposed PaKA framework demonstrates a significant advantage in both computational efficiency and performance enhancement, as shown in Table 14. Our method achieves substantial performance improvements over the DINOv2R baseline while requiring 15% less GPU computation time for post-training compared to NeCo. More impressively, PaKA’s performance gains over DINOv2R are consistently larger than those achieved by NeCo across all tasks. For example, in K=300K=300 overclustering, PaKA boosts performance by 25.225.2 mIoU points over DINOv2R, whereas NeCo achieves a 17.417.4 mIoU gain. This trend continues in end-to-end finetuning segmentation, where PaKA shows a +1.3+1.3 mIoU improvement compared to NeCo’s +0.4+0.4 mIoU, demonstrating PaKA’s superior learning capability even with reduced training overhead.

Appendix F Qualitative Evaluations

F.1 Dense Nearest Neighbor Retrieval

Figure 3, derived from our visual in-context learning evaluation on Pascal VOC, illustrates PaKA’s superior semantic understanding in dense nearest patch retrieval compared to DINOv2R. For each query patch, the top five nearest neighbors are retrieved from the dataset. A striking example is when a query patch depicting an airplane tail is presented: DINOv2R retrieves largely irrelevant patches, such as a bicycle wheel and horses. In contrast, PaKA for the same query retrieves highly relevant patches of airplane tails, reflecting its deeper understanding of patch-level semantics and object structure.

F.2 Overclustering

To qualitatively assess the semantic grouping capabilities inherent in different encoders, we generate visualizations directly from their features without any decoders or finetuning. The process begins by extracting dense patch-level features from validation images using the frozen model backbone. These features then undergo dimensionality reduction via Principal Component Analysis before being grouped using K-Means overclustering. This yields a low resolution map where each patch is assigned a raw cluster ID. To facilitate semantic interpretation, these raw clusters are matched to ground-truth semantic classes using a many-to-one mapping that maximizes IoU. The resulting visualizations in  Figure 4 visually confirm that PaKA yields significantly cleaner clusters that better adhere to object boundaries and capture fine-grained details, outperforming both DINOv2R and NeCo in this qualitative assessment.

Appendix G Dataset Details

Pascal VOC 2012 [28]

The Pascal VOC 2012 presents natural images primarily centered on everyday objects, providing clear examples for object recognition and segmentation. This dataset (trainaug split) provides 10,582 training and 1,449 validation images, covering 21 semantic classes including background.

COCO [29]

COCO images depict complex everyday scenes, often featuring multiple objects in their natural context with varying scales and significant occlusions. This dataset provides 118,000 training images and 5,000 validation images, annotated across 80 distinct object categories. In our work, we utilize the train2017 and val2017 splits from the COCO dataset.

COCO-Stuff 164K [32]

The COCO-Stuff 164K dataset features complex, everyday scenes densely populated with multiple distinct objects ("thing") and large, amorphous regions ("stuff"). It includes detailed annotations for 91 "stuff" categories and 80 "thing" categories. Following [13], , we consolidate these into a reduced set of 15 "stuff" and 12 "thing" classes for our evaluations.

ADE20K [31]

The ADE20K dataset is recognized for its challenging and diverse scenes, featuring highly detailed annotations. It includes 20,210 images in its training set and 2,000 images for validation. The dataset encompasses 150 unique semantic categories, covering a wide array of "stuff" (e.g., sky, grass) and "objects" (e.g., person, car). The "others" label is excluded from our evaluations.
